Prime Counting Function \(\pi(x)\)

primeCount.Rd

Count the prime numbers less than or equal to \(n\), using automatic selection or an explicitly selected Legendre, Meissel, or Lehmer method.

Usage

primeCount(n, nThreads = NULL, method = "auto")

Arguments

n

A single positive whole number, at most \(2^{53} - 1\).

nThreads

Requested number of threads. The default is NULL for serial execution. Requests are capped by the available hardware and the useful work in the calculation. Small or simple cases may use fewer threads. For n < 100000, this argument is ignored and execution is serial.

method

One of "auto", "legendre", "meissel", or "lehmer". Matching is case-sensitive and accepts unique abbreviations, as in match.arg. NULL selects "auto".

Details

Method selection

The current "auto" policy selects a method using n and the usable thread budget, which is the requested number of threads capped by the available hardware:

  • For n < 100000, use small lookup values or a sieve.

  • For 100000 <= n < 10^10, use Legendre's formula.

  • For n >= 10^10, use Meissel's formula, except that inputs n >= 10^12 with at least six usable threads use Lehmer's formula.

These choices are based on first-call and warmed-call benchmarks. They do not depend on the current cache contents, and they do not guarantee the fastest method for every input or machine. The policy may change with further benchmarking. In particular, a method that improves repeated calls can have a slower first call.

An explicit method uses the named algorithm for every accepted n, including small inputs. The method argument follows nThreads, so existing positional calls such as primeCount(n, 2) retain their meaning. All methods use serial execution when nThreads = NULL.

Counting formulas

Let \(p_a\) be the \(a\)th prime, and let \(\Phi(n, a)\) count the positive integers at most \(n\) that are not divisible by any of the first \(a\) primes. Its recurrence is $$\Phi(n, a) = \Phi(n, a - 1) - \Phi(\lfloor n / p_a \rfloor, a - 1)$$ with \(\Phi(n, 0) = n\).

For \(k = 2\) or \(3\), let \(P_k(n, a)\) count integers at most \(n\) with exactly \(k\) prime factors, none among the first \(a\) primes. Factors are counted with multiplicity: \(p^2\) is included in \(P_2\), and \(p^3\) and \(p^2 q\) are included in \(P_3\) when their factors exceed the cutoff. Nondecreasing factor order counts each integer once. When \(a = 0\), all primes are allowed.

The methods use different cutoffs and correction terms:

  • Legendre uses \(a = \pi(\lfloor \sqrt n \rfloor)\): $$\pi(n) = \Phi(n, a) + a - 1.$$

  • Meissel uses \(a = \pi(\lfloor n^{1/3} \rfloor)\): $$\pi(n) = \Phi(n, a) + a - 1 - P_2(n, a).$$

  • Lehmer uses \(a = \pi(\lfloor n^{1/4} \rfloor)\): $$\pi(n) = \Phi(n, a) + a - 1 - P_2(n, a) - P_3(n, a).$$

The Legendre implementation and shared \(\Phi\) calculation build on Kim Walisch's work in primecount, including cached partial-sieve values, small-prime periodic tables, and prime-count lookup shortcuts.

Note

The counting methods prepare tables with storage proportional to \(\sqrt n\). At the maximum input \(2^{53} - 1\), the dense prime-count table requires about 362 MiB and the prime-vector reservation requests about 42 MiB, before caches and other overhead. These are calculated storage estimates, not measured peak memory. Workers within one call share the tables; concurrent calls prepare separate tables. The supported numeric range does not guarantee that every input is practical for available memory.

References

  • Tomás Oliveira e Silva, Computing \(\pi(x)\): the combinatorial method, Revista do DETUA, vol. 4, no. 6, March 2006, p. 761.

  • 53-bit significand precision

Value

A single whole number giving the number of primes less than or equal to \(n\). The result has type integer when it is at most .Machine$integer.max, and type double otherwise. The count is exact throughout the supported range.

Author

Joseph Wood

See also

primeSieve, nthPrime, primePhi, semiPrimeCount, triPrimeCount

Examples

## Get the number of primes less than or equal to a billion
primeCount(10^9)
#> [1] 50847534

## Select a method explicitly
primeCount(10^6, method = "legendre")
#> [1] 78498
primeCount(10^6, method = "meissel")
#> [1] 78498
primeCount(10^6, method = "lehmer")
#> [1] 78498

## Using nThreads
system.time(primeCount(10^10, nThreads = 2, method = "lehmer"))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   0.011   0.000   0.006
